Chapter 7: Parenting Without Bribes or Threats
Picture this: It’s the end of a long day, you’re tired, and all you want is a little peace. So, you toss out a quick deal—“If you clean your room, you can have dessert.” Or maybe, “If you don’t stop fighting, you’ll lose your screen time.”
Sound familiar? These little bargains and threats can feel like lifesavers in the moment. But after a while, something starts to change. Suddenly, your kid is asking, “What do I get if I do it?” or “What happens if I don’t?” It’s like every interaction turns into a negotiation, and somehow, the joy of just being together gets buried under all the deals and warnings.
Some parents, completely worn out by this cycle, start looking for another way. What if, instead of rewards and punishments, you focused on connection and understanding? Imagine this: your child refuses to do a chore. Instead of threatening or bribing, you sit down and ask, “What’s going on?” or “How can we work together to solve this?”
Suddenly, the whole conversation shifts. Your child feels truly heard, and you get a window into what’s really happening beneath the surface.
There’s a story from one family that really brings this to life. Their child was always dragging their feet at bedtime. The usual go-to—offering a treat for getting ready quickly—just wasn’t working. So instead, the parent asked, “What makes bedtime hard for you?” The answer? The child felt lonely after lights out.
Together, they came up with a new routine: a few extra minutes of reading together before sleep. The bedtime struggle faded. And in its place? A real sense of closeness.
Here’s what stands out: when kids feel respected and involved, they’re so much more willing to cooperate. The focus shifts—from just getting them to comply, to actually building a connection. It’s less about control, and more about working together. Your role as a parent isn’t just about managing behavior; it’s about creating a relationship where you both feel valued.
Now, let’s be real—this doesn’t mean letting your kids do whatever they want. Boundaries and expectations still matter. But instead of using power to enforce them, you can invite your child into the process.
Try asking, “What do you think is fair?” or “How can we make this work for everyone?” These questions don’t just solve the immediate problem—they open the door to empathy and real problem-solving.
Most of us don’t realize just how much kids crave a sense of agency. When you trust them to help make decisions, they often rise to the occasion. The need for bribes and threats? It fades away, replaced by a genuine sense of partnership. Home starts to feel like a place where everyone’s needs matter, and where love isn’t something you have to earn.
So, what’s the real reward here? It’s a relationship built on trust, respect, and understanding. When your child feels seen and heard, you don’t have to bribe or threaten them to do their part. They want to help—not for a prize, but because they care about the family.
